intro: Hi again! You can already count to 20 — today we go all the way to 100 and use numbers in real life: your age, your phone number and prices in rupiah. Warm-up: how do you say 20 in English?
teachingNotes: Stress is the whole difference between -teen and -ty: thirTEEN (13), fourTEEN (14) vs THIRty (30), FORty (40). Learners say them the same way — exaggerate the stress and teach the check question 'One-three or three-zero?'.
Spelling: forty has no u (four → forty), and 21–99 take a hyphen in writing (twenty-one, fifty-six). 100 = one hundred or a hundred.
Age uses be, not have: 'I'm 25 (years old)'. Never 'I have 25 years (old)'. 'I'm 25 years' without 'old' is not natural — teach 'I'm 25' or 'I'm 25 years old'. Ask with 'How old are you?'.

Phone numbers are read one digit at a time in small groups with pauses (0812 5567 3490 = oh-eight-one-two, five-five-six-seven, three-four-nine-oh). 0 = 'oh' or 'zero'; 'double five' for 55 is optional. Never read them as big numbers.

Prices: after a number, thousand and hundred never take -s (twenty-five thousand, not 'twenty-five thousands'), and rupiah has no -s. English writes 25,000 with a comma where Indonesian writes 25.000 with a dot. Chunks: 'How much is it?' — 'It's 25,000 rupiah.'
Limits: stay at or below a hundred thousand rupiah; no millions, decimals or years. Grammar only through fixed chunks (I'm…, My number is…, It's…, How much is it?); no past tense.

keyPoints.title: Numbers 21–100
keyPoints.explanation: The tens end in -ty (think 'puluh'): twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, ninety, then one hundred. A few are spelled differently from the small number (two → twenty, three → thirty, four → forty, five → fifty): just learn them. For 21–99 say the ten, then the unit, with a hyphen (-) in writing. -teen numbers (think 'belas') are said strongest at the end (thirTEEN), -ty numbers at the start (THIRty).

keyPoints.title: Your age and phone number
keyPoints.explanation: For age, say I'm (= I am) + the number, and add 'years old' if you like (both words together). In English your age is something you are, not something you have, so don't use have. Read phone numbers one digit at a time, in small groups; 0 is 'oh' or 'zero'.

keyPoints.title: Prices in rupiah
keyPoints.explanation: Say how many thousand, then 'thousand rupiah'. After a number, thousand and hundred have no -s: they are part of the number, like 'ribu' in 'dua ribu'. English writes 25,000 with a comma; Indonesian writes 25.000 with a dot.

blocks.text: You already know 1–20. Now learn the **tens**. They all end in **-ty**, which works like Indonesian **puluh**: *six* → **sixty** (enam → enam puluh). For the numbers in between, say the ten and then the unit, just like Indonesian: **twenty-one** = dua puluh satu, **ninety-nine** = sembilan puluh sembilan. In writing, put a **hyphen** (the short line **-**) between them: *forty-six*. After ninety-nine comes **one hundred** (or **a hundred**).

id.text: Kamu sudah tahu 1–20. Sekarang pelajari **puluhan**. Semuanya berakhiran **-ty**, yang fungsinya mirip kata **puluh**: *six* → **sixty** (enam → enam puluh). Untuk angka di antaranya, sebut puluhannya lalu satuannya, sama seperti bahasa Indonesia: **twenty-one** = dua puluh satu, **ninety-nine** = sembilan puluh sembilan. Saat menulis, beri **tanda hubung** (garis pendek **-**) di antaranya: *forty-six*. Setelah ninety-nine ada **one hundred** (atau **a hundred**).

rows.id: dua puluh satu · lima puluh enam · sembilan puluh sembilan

blocks.text:
**Some tens look different from the small number.** Most are easy: *six* → sixty, *seven* → seventy, *nine* → ninety. But five of them change their spelling, and there is no rule for it. You just have to remember them:
- two → **twenty** (not 'twoty')
- three → **thirty** (not 'threety')
- four → **forty** (no u! not 'fourty')
- five → **fifty** (not 'fivety')
- eight → **eighty** (only one t)

The same happens with the -teen numbers you already know: *thirteen, fifteen, eighteen*.

id.text:
**Ada puluhan yang bentuknya berbeda dari angka satuannya.** Kebanyakan gampang: *six* → sixty, *seven* → seventy, *nine* → ninety. Tapi lima puluhan ini ejaannya berubah, dan tidak ada aturannya. Cukup dihafalkan saja:
- two → **twenty** (bukan 'twoty')
- three → **thirty** (bukan 'threety')
- four → **forty** (tanpa u! bukan 'fourty')
- five → **fifty** (bukan 'fivety')
- eight → **eighty** (huruf t-nya cuma satu)

Hal yang sama terjadi di angka -teen yang sudah kamu kenal: *thirteen, fifteen, eighteen*.

blocks.text:
**thirteen or thirty?** Think **-teen = belas** and **-ty = puluh**. The two sound almost the same, so English uses **stress** to tell them apart. Stress means the part of the word you say **louder and a little longer**. (In Indonesian we say every part of a word about the same; in English one part is strong.)
- -teen numbers are strong at the **end**: thir**TEEN**, fif**TEEN** (tiga belas, lima belas).
- -ty numbers are strong at the **start**: **THIR**ty, **FIF**ty (tiga puluh, lima puluh).

Not sure what you heard? Ask: *One-three or three-zero?*

id.text:
**thirteen atau thirty?** Ingat: **-teen = belas** dan **-ty = puluh**. Bunyi keduanya hampir sama, jadi bahasa Inggris memakai **tekanan** untuk membedakannya. Tekanan artinya bagian kata yang diucapkan **lebih keras dan sedikit lebih panjang**. (Di bahasa Indonesia semua bagian kata diucapkan kira-kira sama kuat; di bahasa Inggris ada satu bagian yang kuat.)
- Angka -teen kuat di **akhir**: thir**TEEN**, fif**TEEN** (tiga belas, lima belas).
- Angka -ty kuat di **awal**: **THIR**ty, **FIF**ty (tiga puluh, lima puluh).

Ragu dengan yang kamu dengar? Tanyakan: *One-three or three-zero?* (satu-tiga atau tiga-nol?)

blocks.prompt: How do you write 40 in words?
blocks.explain: 40 is forty: no u, even though 4 is four. This is one of the tens you just have to remember. Fourteen is 14.

id.explain: 40 adalah forty: tanpa u, walaupun 4 ditulis four. Ini salah satu puluhan yang memang harus dihafal. Fourteen itu 14.

blocks.text:
To give your age, say **I'm** + the number. **I'm** is the short form of **I am** (saya adalah). You can add **years old**, always both words together: *I'm 25* or *I'm 25 years old* (not *I'm 25 years*). For other people, use **is**: *My sister is 17*.

Why not *have*? In English your age is something you **are**, not something you **have**. So *I have 25 years* sounds wrong, like saying 'saya memiliki 25 tahun'. To ask someone, say **How old are you?** (literally 'seberapa tua kamu?', but it just means 'berapa umurmu?').

id.text:
Untuk menyebut umur, katakan **I'm** + angkanya. **I'm** adalah bentuk pendek dari **I am** (saya adalah). Boleh ditambah **years old**, selalu dua kata itu bersama: *I'm 25* atau *I'm 25 years old* (bukan *I'm 25 years*). Untuk orang lain, pakai **is**: *My sister is 17*.

Kenapa bukan *have*? Dalam bahasa Inggris, umur adalah keadaan dirimu (kamu **adalah** 25 tahun), bukan sesuatu yang kamu **punya**. Jadi *I have 25 years* terdengar salah, seperti bilang 'saya memiliki 25 tahun'. Untuk bertanya, katakan **How old are you?** (kalau diterjemahkan kata per kata 'seberapa tua kamu?', tapi artinya cukup 'berapa umurmu?').

blocks.text: Read a phone number **one digit at a time** (satu angka demi satu angka), in small groups with a short pause between them. Never read it as one big number. Say 0 as **oh** (because 0 looks like the letter O) or **zero**: both are fine. Two same digits together can be **double**: 55 = *double five*. This is optional; *five five* is fine too.

id.text: Baca nomor telepon **satu angka demi satu angka**, dalam kelompok kecil dengan jeda singkat di antaranya. Jangan dibaca sebagai satu angka besar. Angka 0 dibaca **oh** (karena 0 mirip huruf O) atau **zero**: dua-duanya benar. Dua angka sama berurutan boleh dibaca **double**: 55 = *double five*. Ini tidak wajib; *five five* juga benar.

blocks.prompt: Choose the right answer to: How old are you?
blocks.explain: Age uses I'm (I am), not I have: in English you are 19, you don't have 19. 'My age 19' is missing the little word is, and English doesn't leave it out.

id.explain: Umur memakai I'm (I am), bukan I have: dalam bahasa Inggris kamu 'adalah' 19 tahun, bukan 'punya' 19 tahun. 'My age 19' tidak punya kata kecil is, padahal bahasa Inggris tidak boleh menghilangkannya.

blocks.text: Rupiah prices are big numbers, but they're easy: say how many **thousand**, then **rupiah**. *Rp25.000* = **twenty-five thousand rupiah** (dua puluh lima *ribu*). With hundreds: *Rp2.500* = **two thousand five hundred rupiah**. To ask the price, say **How much is it?** — **It's 15,000 rupiah.**

id.text: Harga dalam rupiah memang angka besar, tapi mudah: sebut berapa **thousand** (ribu), lalu **rupiah**. *Rp25.000* = **twenty-five thousand rupiah** (dua puluh lima *ribu*). Dengan ratusan: *Rp2.500* = **two thousand five hundred rupiah**. Untuk menanyakan harga, katakan **How much is it?** — **It's 15,000 rupiah.**

rows.note: a hundred thousand / one hundred thousand rupiah

blocks.text: Two common mistakes. First, after a number, **thousand** and **hundred** never take -s: *twenty-five thousand*, not *twenty-five thousands*. Why, when English says *two books* with -s? Because here thousand is **part of the number**, just like *ribu* in *dua puluh lima ribu*. You count books, but thousand is not a thing you count. **rupiah** has no -s either. Second, English writes **25,000** with a **comma**, while Indonesian writes **25.000** with a dot. Same number, different mark.

id.text: Dua kesalahan umum. Pertama, setelah angka, **thousand** dan **hundred** tidak pernah diberi -s: *twenty-five thousand*, bukan *twenty-five thousands*. Kenapa, padahal bahasa Inggris bilang *two books* dengan -s? Karena di sini thousand adalah **bagian dari angkanya**, sama seperti *ribu* di *dua puluh lima ribu*. Buku adalah benda yang dihitung, tapi thousand bukan benda. **rupiah** juga tanpa -s. Kedua, bahasa Inggris menulis **25,000** dengan **koma**, sedangkan bahasa Indonesia menulis **25.000** dengan titik. Angkanya sama, tandanya berbeda.

blocks.text: **a hundred = seratus, a thousand = seribu.** Here **a** means 'one', like **se-** in *seratus* and *seribu*. So *a hundred thousand* = seratus ribu. *One hundred* means the same; *a hundred* is just more common when you speak.

id.text: **a hundred = seratus, a thousand = seribu.** Di sini **a** artinya 'satu', seperti **se-** di *seratus* dan *seribu*. Jadi *a hundred thousand* = seratus ribu. *One hundred* artinya sama; *a hundred* hanya lebih sering dipakai saat berbicara.

blocks.explain: After a number, thousand has no -s, because it is part of the number (like 'ribu' in 'empat puluh lima ribu'): forty-five thousand rupiah.

id.explain: Setelah angka, thousand tidak diberi -s, karena thousand adalah bagian dari angkanya (seperti 'ribu' di 'empat puluh lima ribu'): forty-five thousand rupiah.

material.title: At the warung and on the road

blocks.text: When you shop or travel, numbers are everywhere: prices, room numbers, bus numbers, phone numbers. Listen carefully, and **repeat the number back** to check it. Even native speakers do this all the time.

id.text: Saat belanja atau bepergian, angka ada di mana-mana: harga, nomor kamar, nomor bus, nomor telepon. Dengarkan baik-baik, lalu **ulangi angkanya** untuk memastikan. Penutur asli pun selalu melakukannya.

rows.en: How much is the nasi goreng? — It's 22,000 rupiah.

rows.id: Maaf, lima belas atau lima puluh?

blocks.text: Check a phone number by reading it back in groups: *Oh-eight-one-two … five-five-six-seven?* If one digit is wrong, the other person can fix it quickly.

id.text: Pastikan nomor telepon dengan membacanya ulang per kelompok: *Oh-eight-one-two … five-five-six-seven?* Kalau ada satu angka yang salah, lawan bicara bisa langsung membetulkannya.
